video_caption: In a lab setting, a person wearing light blue surgical gloves holds a dissected animal heart (likely a cow or pig heart) over a blue dissection tray, which is placed inside a larger, beige tray. A pair of silver scissors rests on the blue tray to the right. The person uses a slender, curved metal probe to point at different parts of the heart's exterior, specifically highlighting a sulcus or wrinkle on what they identify as the posterior view of the heart to distinguish the right and left ventricles.

A person wearing blue gloves holds a heart specimen over a blue dissection tray. They insert a silver probe into the superior end of the heart, then use a pair of small silver scissors to cut along the probe, opening up a chamber of the heart. After removing the probe, they use their gloved hands to gently pull apart the cut edges of the heart, revealing the internal structure of the right atrium. The scissors and probe are placed on the blue tray beside the heart.

In a video segment displaying an anatomy lesson, a person wearing light blue examination gloves holds a dissected heart specimen over a blue mat within a grey dissection tray on a dark countertop. The person carefully opens the heart lengthwise to reveal its internal chambers. They then use a silver metal dissection probe to point to specific anatomical features. First, the probe indicates the upper chamber, which the speaker identifies as the right atrium. Next, the probe is moved downwards to highlight the lower chamber, identified as the right ventricle. The person then uses their gloved finger and the probe to demonstrate and emphasize the notable thickness of the right ventricle's wall, verbally noting its role as a stronger pump compared to the thinner-walled atrium, which the probe subsequently points to for comparison.

In a close-up shot, a person wearing light blue gloves holds a dissected biological specimen, likely a heart, in their left hand, resting it on a light gray dissection tray with a blue interior. The heart is cut open, revealing its internal structures. With their right hand, the person uses a silver, pointed dissection tool to gently manipulate and point at thin, string-like structures within the specimen. To the right, a pair of small silver scissors or forceps also lies in the tray. The background is a dark, smooth surface, suggesting a laboratory setting.

In a close-up shot, two hands, clad in light blue latex gloves, hold a dissected anatomical heart specimen over a rectangular blue dissection tray, which rests on a dark tabletop. The left hand firmly grips the heart, while the right hand manipulates a slender, silver-colored probe to point at various internal structures. Initially, the probe points to the outer surface of the heart, identified as the epicardium. The right hand then shifts the probe to indicate a thicker, more muscular central layer, described as the myocardium. Finally, the probe moves to highlight the thin, shiny innermost lining, the endocardium, as the left hand subtly adjusts the heart's position to better reveal this detail. A pair of small silver scissors lies in the dissection tray to the right of the heart throughout the segment.

In a close-up shot, a pair of hands, gloved in light blue, are meticulously dissecting a heart, likely a specimen for anatomical study. The heart is opened, revealing its internal structures. One gloved hand holds the heart steady, while the other skillfully uses a slender metal probe to point to a distinct, dark muscular band stretching across the inner right side of the heart. A pair of small, sharp dissection scissors rests on the blue insert of a light gray dissection tray, which holds the specimen on a dark surface, characteristic of a laboratory setting. Around the 0:26 mark, the hands carefully turn the heart over, presenting a different external view of the organ.

A person wearing light blue gloves holds a dissected heart specimen over a light blue dissection tray. The heart has been cut open, revealing its internal structures. Initially, the person holds the heart to show its posterior view, indicating the right atrium and right ventricle, which are visible through an opening made earlier. Then, the person rotates the heart to its anterior view. Using a silver metal probe, they point to a large vessel on the anterior side, identifying it as the pulmonary trunk. They insert the probe into the pulmonary trunk, demonstrating its connection to the right ventricle by flipping the heart back to its posterior view, showing the probe emerging from the right ventricle. A pair of silver scissors is also visible in the tray.

In a lab setting, a person wearing light blue gloves carefully dissects a biological heart specimen, likely from an animal, which is placed in a light gray tray with a blue mat. Initially, a metal probe is inserted into a vessel at the top of the heart, with the probe extending through to the heart's surface. The person uses small silver dissection scissors to make an incision along the length of the heart, following the path indicated by the probe. They skillfully turn the heart to gain better access, continuing the cut deeply into the organ to open up the right side towards the right ventricle. The incision eventually separates a significant portion of the heart, revealing internal structures, as the person completes the cut while still holding the probe and scissors.

A person wearing light blue medical gloves is shown from an overhead perspective, carefully dissecting a pale-colored organ, likely a heart, on a blue silicone mat within a light grey dissection tray. The gloved hands hold the organ, and a silver metal probe is inserted into one of its vessels. The person uses their hands to gently pull apart the tissue, revealing the internal structure of the vessel where the probe is positioned. A pair of small silver surgical scissors or forceps rests on the blue mat to the right of the heart. The dissection takes place on a dark, flat surface.

In a close-up shot, a person wearing light blue gloves carefully holds a dissected heart in their left hand, resting it on a blue mat within a beige dissection tray. With their right hand, they use a silver dissection probe to point inside the heart's chambers. The heart appears to be a mammalian heart, possibly a pig or sheep heart, cut open longitudinally to expose its internal structures. A pair of silver dissection scissors is visible on the blue mat to the right of the heart. The person points the probe toward a valve, identifying it verbally as a "semilunar valve," then moves the probe deeper into what they describe as the "right ventricle," and subsequently points out a "moderator band." The background is a dark, possibly black, tabletop.

In a close-up shot, a person wearing light blue disposable gloves holds a heart specimen, likely a mammalian heart used for dissection, in a light grey dissecting tray with a blue mat. With their right gloved hand, they hold a silver dissecting probe, using its tip to point to and gently manipulate a part of the heart's upper structure, which appears to be a valve or a cusp. Their left gloved hand firmly holds the heart. A pair of silver scissors rests on the blue mat to the right of the heart. The background is a dark, out-of-focus surface, suggesting a lab or educational setting.
